released: not yet: the v2.0.0rc3 tag's own creation date, to be filled in when the tag is cut. The tag does not exist in this repository yet, so there is nothing to record here -- and a date written before the tag existed would be one that never happened.
released_as: not yet: the commit the v2.0.0rc3 tag will point at, to be filled in when the tag is cut. Left empty on purpose rather than guessed. Every other released_as in this directory names a commit that is in this repository and can be checked with git; a plausible-looking hash here would be the one entry that could not be, and 1.1.0.json's entire argument is that the commit is the part that has to be real. Two fields are to be filled in at that moment and only these two: released and released_as.
why_there_is_no_record: Not measured, and this is a rehearsal like the two before it. rc3 exists because rc2 built cleanly and then failed one job later. rc2's build succeeded on all three platforms and uploaded an artifact from each, and its release job -- the one that assembles the archives, writes the SBOM, hashes what ships and creates the Release page -- died on ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml', thrown by tools/release_checksums.py. That job declared an interpreter and no dependencies, and it acquired two Python steps in a milestone that added the SBOM and the checksums without anyone noticing the job had nothing installed for them; a job that runs only on a tag installs nothing until the tag, so no pull request could have seen it. rc2 therefore has downloadable artifacts and no GitHub Release page. rc3 is cut to run the whole thing -- build and release assembly -- end to end, which is the part of the pipeline no green build had exercised. No sweep runs at this tag either: benchmarks/perf_baseline.py and benchmarks/compare/run_comparison.py are not executed at an rc, for the reason 1.2.1.json gives.
the_defect_is_repaired_and_now_has_a_pul: The repair has two halves. The release job installs pyyaml and nothing else, because release_checksums.py reads the release's files: globs with it and the three other tools the job runs are standard library only. The half worth recording is the guard: tools/ci_selfcheck.py deps now runs as part of shape on every ordinary pull request, and for every job that runs a tools/*.py script it reads that script's third-party imports with ast and fails unless the job's own interpreter installs something that provides them. It has to get two things right to be worth having, and does: an install into a sibling venv is not the job's environment, or the release job's throwaway SBOM venv would have stood in for its own PyYAML and the check would have passed on the broken tree; and an import guarded by an except that recovers is not a requirement, or the static ci-shape job would be asked to install Qt. This is the first time a class of defect that only ever fires on a tag -- a step whose dependency was never installed because no earlier ref ran it -- has had anything watching it before the tag, rather than after. What the guard cannot prove is that the tag itself will be green; only the tag can, which is what rc3 is for.
how_this_differs_from_the_two_before_it: All three entries are recorded: false, and the three absences are not the same absence, so this file says which one it is rather than letting a reader infer it. rc1's build died on all three platforms and produced no artifact at all, so there was nothing that could have been measured even in principle -- any figure in that file would have described a binary that does not exist. rc2's build succeeded and produced three downloadable artifacts, and the measurement was never taken; its failure was one job past the build. rc3's build and release assembly are both expected to complete, so that the whole tag-to-Release-page path is proven in one run, and the measurement is again not taken, because a rehearsal is not a measurement point and a sweep at a tag nobody installs would put a number in this directory that describes a commit rather than a release.
the_evidence_this_entry_waits_on: The v2.0.0rc3 tag's own packaging run, once the tag is cut. Until then there is no run to cite and no result to report, so this entry cites none: released and released_as above are left in the not-yet form on purpose, and the two of them are what a person fills in from git log -1 --format=%aI v2.0.0rc3 and git rev-parse v2.0.0rc3 when the tag exists. The rc2 failure this files is repair for is recorded, with its own evidence, in 2.0.0rc2.json.
no_numbers_were_fabricated_here: Deliberately empty of numbers, for the reason 2.0.0rc1.json gives and one more. Nothing has been measured at this tag, so any figure would describe a run that has not happened. And nothing has even been built yet: the tag does not exist, so this entry cannot cite a byte count or a job result the way 2.0.0rc2.json can cite its own artifacts. The absence here is the strongest of the three -- rc1 at least had a failed build to point at, and rc2 a successful one.
what_would_close_this: The 2.0.0 release, for the same reason 1.2.1.json gives. A release candidate is cut to rehearse the pipeline, and rehearsing the release assembly is what this tag is for; the figures that belong in this directory are the ones taken at a version somebody installs. perf_baseline.py and run_comparison.py now write schema_version, an identity block, the generated dataset's seed and digest, and every individual run's raw values, so the 2.0.0 record will be generated rather than reconstructed. Until then 2.0.0rc3's performance is unknown -- not equal to 2.0.0rc2's or 2.0.0rc1's, which also have no record, and not equal to 1.1.0's, which has one taken six commits past its own tag.
